what: Reload the model at A = 0°. Identify the yellow crank, blue coupler, red upper toggle, orange lower toggle, and orange ram. Watch the ram marker relative to the dark-gray support rail while the program runs once.
try: Use manual jog within −82° to 0°. Compare ram motion over the first 10° of motor travel with ram motion over the final 10° before the −80° target. Never command below −82°.

Before moving, predict whether changing the target from −70° to −80° will add more or less ram travel than changing it from −10° to −20°. Also predict what risk grows as the command approaches −85.46°.
Compare the actual output with your prediction before revealing the explanation.
why: As the knee rises toward the ram line, the lower link becomes almost horizontal. More crank rotation is then spent changing link angle and less appears as ram displacement per degree. That geometric change is why a toggle press can develop high ideal mechanical advantage near dead centre; this model does not measure force.
question: Before moving, predict whether changing the target from −70° to −80° will add more or less ram travel than changing it from −10° to −20°. Also predict what risk grows as the command approaches −85.46°.
answer: The builder predicts 26.2853 mm total ram travel at −80°, with the lower link only 2.9268° from the ram line. The analytical dead-centre pose is near −85.46°, so −80° leaves about 5.46°. Native physics must still verify the actual trajectory and return.
matters: One motor turns a yellow crank. A blue coupler folds the red and orange knee links, pushing an orange ram along two guide rails. The program approaches—but does not cross—dead centre, then returns to the saved datum.
further: Vary the input speed and repeat from the saved datum. Does the geometric law change?
Find the passive output and its real bearings. Which physical connection transmits the drive?
formula: Two equal toggle links constrain the guided ram; compare stroke per equal crank increment.
